transcript.text: And I hope that doesn't happen.
Thanks, Eric. And I see Joanne is joining us too. So we got a little bit of finance committee showing up. That's great. Good morning. Sorry. I put in the wrong code.
Yeah. We heard we heard you a little garbled, Joanne. How are you hearing us? Can you see the screen?
I'm not going to be on camera yet this morning, but thank you for the invitation. I put in the wrong code originally, but I'm glad I'm in now.

Okay, yep. Well, I am not going to delay any more because it's a beautiful Saturday morning out there. So Eric, can you allow me to share my screen and I'll try and get the presentation up here? Okay, so hopefully you can all see the presentation at this point. And it's a small group, so I guess given that, I'm gonna try to take questions as we go. And if there was a larger group, I'd have waited till we're at the end, but I'm gonna go ahead and start. And good morning for those of you who don't know me. I'm Jed Larson and I'm the chairman of the Andover Planning And Zoning Commission. I want to thank you for attending this morning, giving up a beautiful Saturday morning here at Andover in an effort to learn about the plan and your interest in creating affordable housing in Andover. I was hoping Bill Warner would be here. I want to thank him for his help in developing the plan, know, and he's been working with the town of Andover for many years. He was a town planner

a while back and a land use consultant for several of the projects that we've done. So the commission felt we were fortunate with his background of Andover to have us helping him out. And I know Joanne, you and Diane will thank Bill as well. I did show him the presentation ahead of time and his only comment was, wow, that's a lot of slides. So I did eliminate a bunch of them in an effort. I see Jim's notice when it went out talked about a brief presentation and so I wanted to do my best to keep it there. So I eliminated several of the slides and I worked to make the presentation as brief as I can but I have a fair amount of information and so at that point I'll get started. And what we're going to discuss today is we're going to start out with the affordable housing, Diane. What is it? Who needs it?

And what are the Connecticut state statutes that apply? Then we'll talk about the situation in Andover, population trends, that was a little concerning to me, the current housing stock. Is there a need in Andover? In which it Andover's affordable housing goal be? We have several recommendations coming from the Andover affordable housing plan. And lastly, I'm interested in what you folks think. Please mute yourself when you're not talking to keep the background noise down. Presentation was created over the last six months and is a snapshot in time. A lot has changed in the last six months with inflation, higher interest rates, and higher housing prices as well. The result of these factors is that the need for affordable housing continues to grow and become an even more important issue for our town. Over the past six months, my feelings on affordable housing have evolved from not thinking we needed one, to thinking this plan for affordable housing would be good for Andover,

to thinking that if we fail to act on this, we do so at our own peril. I hope I can convince you of that as well. Share your thoughts with others and maybe we'll get a little more interest in this as we go along. We'll start out with Diane's question when she was tuning in here, what is affordable housing? And by the Connecticut state definition, affordable housing is housing that is affordable to individuals and families making 80% or less than the area median income. It also goes on to say that a family at that income level cannot spend more than 30% of their total income on housing, whether that's rent or mortgage taxes and insurance. Andover's median family income is about $105,000 And so what that means to us is that if you take 80% of that 105,000, that's about 80,000. And then if you take 30,000 or 30% of that to be spent on housing, it comes down to about $2,000 a month. If you make less than that 80,000, obviously you've got less to spend on housing. Affordable housing can be rental units or private ownership, and it can be condos, apartments or single family homes. Jed, real quick, the slides are not advancing.
Can you hit the from current slide slideshow and then advance through so we can see visually?
Okay, yep. Thanks for helping me out on that. And let me There we go. Well, so
I guess you'll have to you'll have to see the little bit of stuff off on the left hand side, then maybe this will work and get you where we are there. But anyhow, that's the Jed,
if you just hit the little button up on that says from current slide, that should start the slideshow and then you should be able to go.

Well, let's try it here. When I do that, I lose my, well, we'll see if it goes here. The last thing I wanted to say about the affordable housing for the state definition is an affordable housing unit must be de restricted for forty years so that the value of the house can go up no more than the consumer price index. That's certainly anybody who's out there building a single family home is not going to put a deed restriction on it. That's always been one of the keys to growing your own wealth, if you will, is the ability to have that money in your house. And so that's really going to apply to developments. And then if we have an accessory dwelling unit, the deed restrictions will lay for ten years, so that's a little bit better. Did the slideshow advance to the next picture? It did not. Okay, so I'm gonna go back and we're gonna try it. I'll just do it this way. Now you got a picture of some housing.

Yes, and if you wanted, because I have the presentation, I could probably launch the presentation and you could speak and I could just advance the slides if you want to try that. I prefer to do this. I've been working on the presentation

since I sent it to you and I think that would probably confuse me a little more than that. Anyhow, here are some pictures of privately developed affordable housing. And in our plan, we're talking about quality housing that we should be proud to have in our community. The housing may be a little smaller, the lots a little closer together, but we're talking about very nice housing and what many people would desire today. As we went through this, it occurred to me that maybe the American dream with respect to housing is changing just a little bit. You know, when the baby boomers like me were

entering the housing market, we all thought we wanted, at least a lot of us thought we wanted big houses on big lots to raise a family. This might not be true today. Economic, social, and environmental issues point towards a desire for smaller houses on smaller lives with less maintenance. Hopefully we advance to a picture of what we're not talking about. In the majority of affordable housing is concentrated in the cities. Here are some pictures of public housing which exists to serve those in the very low income brackets. These are heavily subsidized and such subsidies are not targeted to rural areas because of a lack of need and lack of infrastructure to support such population, including public sewers, water, and transportation. So back in 1989, Connecticut recognized that the state was having an affordable housing problem and adopted Connecticut General Statute eight-thirty gs, which required each town to have 10% of its housing deemed affordable per the state definition. Andover is not the only town that struggled to meet that 10% wicket in Connecticut. And in fact, most of the smaller towns are in the same boat that Andover has been in with much smaller number of affordable homes than which are acquired. So Andover is subject to the provisions of eight thirty gs because we're required to have the 10% of our housing units affordable and we're not.

And what eight thirty gs specifies is that developers, when they come in and build the development, at least 30% of those units will be designated as affordable. That is affordable to the people making less than 80% of the median income and only spending 30% of their income on housing. And in fact, 15% of those that are designated as affordable will be affordable to families making 60% of the median income. In the significance of eight-thirty gs is it allows developers to disregard zoning rules while also shifting the burden of proof to the town to justify a denial. So while our zoning regs require about an acre and a half of land in 200 foot of frontage and all these things to make developments. Somebody coming in to develop under eight thirty gs can disregard all those requirements and build whatever kind of housing development they want, as long as it passes the public health code. So it becomes very difficult for a town to deny an application which does not meet current zoning standards but does meet the minimum standards found in the act which says public health code has to buy into it. So essentially in order to deny an application the town is required to find documented and proven public health or safety concerns. The problem is that no matter how easy it is to gain approval for an affordable housing development, the developer isn't going to develop the property unless he can make a profit in doing so.

So little progress was made in getting the towns to create affordable housing. And in 2017, the Connecticut General Statute eight-30J was adopted. And this says that at least once every five years, each municipality shall prepare or amend and adopt an affordable housing plan for the municipality. Such plan shall specify how the municipality intends to increase the number of affordable housing developments in the municipality. It doesn't say what needs to be in the plan, doesn't say what's required or who adopts it, and no public hearing is required. So at this point, the Planning and Zoning Commission has drafted up this plan based on any feedback we get today. We might tweak on it a little bit but this is our plan. Last year Connecticut recognized it as an unfunded mandate to create the plan and use federal money to create a grant program which he took advantage of. We hired Bill Warner and he created the plan with us. And these plans are due to the state by the 06/01/2022, which is coming up soon.

Excuse me, Chad. Yep. Are we able to ask the questions as we go along? Yep, go ahead. Okay, just a quick question on a couple of the slides back. Have we identified, I mean, overall already I'm very interested and I think it's, you know, with the times we're in in the country and everything we see in town and the state will be a good idea for Andover. But have we identified plots of land
or does that come later in your presentation? I don't want to jump my questions. Nope, that does come a little bit later. We'll talk about a couple of places that
Down drafted a an incentive housing plan in '17 and it's got a couple of examples we'll talk about. Okay, I don't want to jump in. I just don't want to skip the chance to ask Okay, my

no, very good, thank you. But anyhow, and I don't know how closely you know all of you have followed all the news on planning and zoning stuff from the state capital, but last year Public Act 20 one-twenty nine was adopted in the legislature was going to take all this action to force the towns to create affordable housing. There was a lot of pushback from the towns and there's a bunch of stuff in that act that the Planning and Zoning Commission is going to be dealing with, but there were two items that really pertained to affordable housing that I wanted to talk about today. The first was the accessory dwelling units, and these are you know the little extra apartments if you will that can be internal to the house, external to the house. Know when we first put the accessory dwelling unit regulation into our zoning regs, I remember the discussion at the time was this was for our aging parents or a caregiver or something like that. And since then, it's come to show that the accessory dwelling units can be a good source of affordable housing, especially for the young folks just starting out. And you know I have a son that lived in essentially an accessory dwelling unit down in Groton next to Electric Boat where he's working and he got his start. And I go back to you know the TV show Happy Days, which I watched and Fonzie lived in, you know, the accessory dwelling unit there. So anyhow, accessory dwelling units can be a good thing for the town, but the state mandated that each town shall designate locations and zoning districts within the municipality in which accessory apartments are allowed,

provided, and this is the important part, provided at least one accessory apartment shall be allowed as of right on each lot that contains a single family dwelling. So there's some words in the public act that allow us to opt out for the accessory dwelling units, and while I think there's a lot of good stuff in there that we may want to take a look at, I don't think the town of Andover wants to have people building accessory dwelling units on the very small lots on Andover Lake because of the detriment that could cause the lake. So anyhow, we'll take a look there. We've also got to figure out how do we go about making it attractive for people who are building an accessory dwelling unit to want to have a ten year deed restriction on that. You know, if you have your parents living in the house with you, ten years might not be all that excessive and that big a deal, but you know to have a deed restrict for ten years, we've got to provide incentive for the people that want to sign that. I don't know exactly how to do that but we'll figure it out. The other thing that was in the public act was that it allowed manufactured mobile homes that exceed 22 feet in their narrowest dimension in towns. Know, mobile homes have long been viewed as affordable housing distracting from the character that the towns are trying to maintain. And so Andover, like most small towns, currently prohibits mobile homes and mobile home parks, and we'll need to change that to be consistent with the Connecticut statute. Okay, so now we're going to look at Andover a little more

specifically. And this slide talks about the median household income by age of householder. And as we started down this path, I was concerned about the seniors. I know we have a lot of seniors in town living on a fixed income. And as you can see, for the people 65 years and over, the average income is down to around 73,000 per year, which is below the, you know, the 80% of the town median, which comes into about 81. The other thing that was interesting on this slide is we must not have very many, if any households with people 25 years of age in there because there's no data there at all. And you can see for overall Pollen County, know, the average, the median income there was like $26,000 So that's pretty small, but certainly if we wanted to attract younger folks to start out in Andover, they're gonna need some help too. The state used median incomes in terms of family size. And I struggled to understand this at first because I was concerned about seniors living on fixed incomes and how did we take care of them and I think the lower senior incomes are reflected in the lower incomes for the smaller

family sizes of one or two people. Anyway, are the numbers that state uses in considering our eligibility for affordable housing. Now let's look at Andover's housing stock and I've got a bunch of statistics here and it probably gets blurred a little bit on what I'm trying to say but bear with me here. You know, we've got thirteen fifty seven housing units in Andover. 92%, which is higher than the surrounding area's average, are single family homes. And of those single family homes, 62% are three or more bedroom homes, which is our families are continuing to get smaller, maybe those aren't what people are looking for today. 82% of our single family homes are owner occupied. And again, that's a much higher number than the state average. So we've only got 12% of those homes as rental units. And at the time the survey was taken, know, there were 7% or 87 units vacant.

So anyhow, to have 10% of our housing affordable, we would require about 132 housing units, which 10% of that top number thirteen fifty seven. We currently have 51 and this is a deficit of about 81 affordable homes. Now let's look at the rental market in Andover. For rental, the state programs use the fair market rent for the region is determined by HUD. And so in this little chart here in the center, can see the different fair market rents by unit bedroom ranging from $670 a month for an efficiency up to about $1,500 a month for a four bedroom house. Down below are the actual rents reported in Andover and you can see we've got 114 units of $500 to $1,000 essentially, and that's the majority of our rental. Dollars 32 are in the $1,000 to $1,500 per month range and 10 are in excess of $1,500 a month. So you look at the rent costs and you say gee whiz, Andover's a great place to live. As we saw from the last slide, you know, problem is there are a few rental options available to people in Andover and they're primarily older homes with more maintenance. Next, I wanted to look at the home ownership. And this slide takes two examples, a family of two and a family of four with the income that the state defined as being 80% of the median for that family size. We're gonna take 30% of it to come up with an actual housing payment of

20,000 per year for a family of 2 or 24,000 for a family of four, which comes down to a monthly payment of about $1,600 a month for a family of two and 2,000 for a family of four. Next we looked at what kind of house can you get for that kind of money and we looked at $250,000 $300,000 and $350,000 And if you take the principal interest, what the taxes would be, add on the insurance, that gives you a total payment for a $250,000 house of about $15.80 dollars per month, which we see that's what a family of two can afford. So that shows that a family of two can go in and get a $250,000 house. That family of four can afford the $300,000 house and family of four didn't make it quite up to the $350,000 So this gets into what we call naturally occurring affordable units in Andover. As I mentioned before, to me, when I moved here, I thought Andover seemed to be a very affordable place to live.

None of these homes have the forty year deed restrictions placed so they don't count towards affordable housing, but you can see you know we've got the last four years worth of numbers here. Total sales, how many of those sales were under $250,000 How many were under $300,000 and that includes those that were under $250,000 And so it shows the percentage of those that are under $300,000 or affordable to a family of four ranging from 78% in 2018 to 57% in 2021. These homes are also older than average and while making them more affordable to buy, more costly to maintain, and less desirable than a newer home. You can also see the trend is toward fewer homes selling for the affordable prices given the recent rapid increase in selling prices. So that's where we are on our housing stock. This is a slide that really got my attention and should be to all of us living in Andover. It shows Andover's population going down. And I thought this might be reflective of the statewide trend of population so I dug a little deeper into that and found that while the population in Connecticut increased slightly from 2019 to 2020 by about 1%, the population in Andover decreased by 87 people or 2.7%. I went back and looked at the last plan of conservation and development and that plan did not anticipate the decline in population. It showed it leveling off

but it did not recognize that it would decline. That document came out in 2015. You look at the numbers of the data that went into that, you know, from 2012 to 2014, it shows it kind of leveling off there and then we're starting to decline again. The Connecticut Data Center projects population to continue to decline further to only 2,864 people in 2030 and 2,550 in 2040. Now we all think Andover is a great place to live, so why is this happening? Should we be concerned and what can we do to change it if we think it's a problem? I go back to the recent long term plan that the town of Andover issued in 2019 which recognized the need and importance for creating affordable housing. It said Andover will have to work hard to attract millennials,

especially homebuyers, to overcome a bias toward more urban amenities. It also went on to state that Andover has 93% single family housing. This will need to change to attract younger demographic. This is coupled with the fact that Andover has very little affordable housing. So anyhow, we've recognized it as a problem like the state recognized it starting back in, you know, the late 1990s. But I think it's something that should be a concern to all of us. Next slide shows the median age in Andover and it happens to be much older than the county and the state in general. This slide also got my attention. We have recognized that Andover has an aging population and again I attributed this to our country's population aging in general with the baby boomer population reaching our senior years. But Andover is aging faster than average. Do we have the housing to support them as they age and desire smaller houses on smaller lots that are easier to maintain? Again from the long term plan the town issued in 2019, Andover's population is aging and without a concerted effort to attract millennial homebuyers this trend will accelerate. And this is where my opinion on affordable housing shifted from something that was nice to do

to something that we had to tackle for the future well-being of our town. This slide shows the number of building permits issued per year from about nineteen ninety to twenty seventeen. We can see the building permits issued peaked in 1996 at about 36 permits that year. Know, things were good, people were building lots of houses, people were buying, moving to Andover, and that sort of thing. For the last ten to twelve years we have been seeing three to five building permits per year. So the speculative market in housing hasn't existed since the housing bubble burst back actually before 2010, probably 02/2008. With that, it's going to be difficult for Andover to reach the 10% goal. In the 90s, we were building 20 to 30 units of housing a year, but from 2009 on, it's been less than 10 and essentially three to five in the last several years. We need 81 additional affordable units to meet our state mandate of 10% affordable. If we were to do this, and if a developer had to make 30% of a development affordable, that means we'd be building two seventy two new units in Andover, 191 at the market rate and 81 affordable. And that's probably not going to happen anytime soon. So Andover will always be subject to that eight-thirty gs requirement. In a lot of towns, there's a very significant gap between the price that the affordable houses sell at and the price that are going at the market rate. That allows those towns to make up for what they're losing on the affordable housing by the prices they're charging on the market rate units. That's not happening here in Andover. In a lot of the small towns, the gap is much narrower. We see if we want affordable housing to mix in well

with the town, it's going to look very similar to the market based sales. So this isn't going to solve our problem for us anytime soon. We've also got the lack of public sewer which makes density very challenging here in Andover. So while we're always going to be subject to the eight-thirty gs regulations, the likelihood of a developer doing an eight thirty gs application in Andover is very small. Next, I wanted to look at who should the affordable housing plan target. And we've talked now about young folks wanting to keep them in town. And this graph of age distribution shows that we've got about four forty three people in the 10 19 year old age bracket. Now those folks aren't going go out and buy homes today, but by the time we get around to actually having some affordable housing, they may be in the marketplace and we'd be interested in keeping those people here in town. The other group that we talked about were the seniors and we see a big bracket from 50 to 69 years of age. We got two little spikes there that show us we've got almost 1,200 empty nesters potentially looking to downsize and stay in town. And if we don't have options for them to stay in town, that means that they're probably going to go someplace else.

So with that, how many units are potentially needed? And somewhere off all the state data, see that 18% of the households in Andover spend between 3050% of their income on housing. On top of that, there's 4% of the households that spend more than half of their income on housing. So for this plan, you know, we took a look at the low end of what is needed, it would be the 4% that spend more than half. And if we went to the upper limit, it would be all the people that spend above 30% of their income on housing. And the same statistics said that the hourly wage needed to afford a two bedroom apartment

is $23.65 down below if we looked at the know the ten to nineteen year old age grouping there were four forty three residents. If we took care of the 4% that are paying more than half that would be 18 residents. If we took a look at the 18% that are between 30 50 that comes up to 80. Similarly with the fifty to sixty nine year olds, know we show that again 4% it comes out to about four fifty households when you take a look at there's about 2.6 people per household. And again on the low end that would be about 18 households, the upper end 81 households. So that gives us a bracket of potential need anywhere from between thirty six and one hundred and sixty one units. The need for affordable housing should not be viewed as something we need to do to meet the state requirement, but as we show here, something we want to tackle to get the young people to want to live here, raise a family here, retire here, and stay here. We really need to have more than our deficit of 81 units that's suggested. So next we'll take a look at the affordable housing units that currently exist. And again, we're supposed to have 10%, which is 133 units basically. In 2015, it shows that we had 24 government assisted

units and 31 units that were financed with the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority or US Department of Agriculture federally subsidized loans for a total of 51 units. That comes out to an affordable rate of 4.18% as opposed to the 10% required. In 2020, we see that the numbers actually went down a little bit and I have not been able to get the light bulb on in my brain successfully on why the government assisted numbers went from 24 to 18. I know there's still 24 units sitting over there on Riverside Drive. Talked to Eric, he tried to help explain that to me a little bit,

but it just doesn't make sense that we should have lost credit for six of our affordable housing units there. But anyhow, you know, we did. I don't know if we can get it back, but anyhow, that has resulted in our drop in affordable housing numbers down to the total of 51 that we have today for 3.85%. So we need 81 additional units to reach the 10%. That brings us to what should we have as a goal in Andover for affordable housing? And our plan came up with we should try to create five to 15 affordable housing units in the next ten years and it should be targeted to Andover seniors interested in downsizing. In Andover's ten to nineteen year old age cohort, which I guess now is generation Z, the generation, the millennial generations, a little bit older than that now. And this sounds like a fairly modest goal in terms of what we need, but could be a very challenging goal to meet in terms of what we have seen for building activity over the past several years. This is where we get into talking about where is the property in Andover that we might be able to develop. And Andover put out an incentive housing zone study in 2017 and essentially came up with three possible sites that we could use. The first is the Phelps property over on Schottie Mill Road and it's about 9.4 acres that we could develop. The next property listed was Rosewood Acres on Lindholt's Corner which is about 16.4 acres. And lastly is the town of Andover property behind the town hall which is about 70 acres. And I wanted to take a little closer look

at the town of Andover property as I consider this a very promising option that because Andover already owns the property, we could make a deal with the developer to get the developer interested in building housing back there. The incentive housing zone created two development scenarios which are displayed in the following figures. And this shows you know several, this shows 10 of those multi unit housing complexes that we saw in the picture right up front. 42 units in 10 buildings with a mixture of one and two bedroom units and I thought that was a very attractive option back there. The other scenario that we looked through was your 24 single family lots of two bedroom homes. And I think this would be a great move forward to the development of the town center concept that our plan of conservation development addresses, especially now that our new senior community center is approaching reality. This would be a great help to those in town who might benefit from increased affordable housing.

So where do we go from here? First, let's look at the organization awareness of the plan. Know, and the first goal was to present the plan. I was hoping that we get a few more takers, but with the weather being so nice out there today, I know that's a tough sell to come listen to a presentation on affordable housing. But hopefully, you people that did attend can help the town out, spreading the word that, this is something we really need to do. And I'm hoping that I get the opportunity to present the plan in additional venues going forward. It's important to recognize that the plan is not free, Doesn't cost very much, but as you can see from the third bullet down there, it's gonna talk about a permanent staff member being assigned to the committee. So we would have to pay for that. Any of the affordable housing that we developed in this plan would add to the grant list, and so it would be a plus for the town budget that way, but it would certainly cost us a little bit to get started. Now, a couple of the things that we did not consider in our plan that other towns have considered, and they're actually putting in the budget the town purchasing property to make it available to developers so that they can go out and build affordable housing. I didn't think that with as hard as we worked to get through a budget to pass, that would be something that we wanted to address right now, so it's not in the plan. Other towns are also going out and buying housing that they are renting to people

to create affordable housing there. With similar thing, I didn't think that was something that we would be looking at getting into our plan right now. However, if the town all of a sudden said, yep, those are great ideas, we should do them, be happy to add those into the plan. Next is create an affordable housing committee. Plans are often shelved because there's no champion. It is recommended that an affordable housing committee be established with the goal of keeping this plan in the forefront. And we're hoping that the Board of Selectmen would be willing to establish that committee. And ideally, a permanent paid town staff member with true interest in this subject could be assigned to staff to the affordable housing committee to help them out. Next, look at what we would like the affordable housing committee to do.

And the committee and the staff could use social media, print media, and presentations to highlight the need and identify and work with residents in need of affordable housing or interested in renovations to agent plays to create affordable accessory units. Perhaps one of the biggest issues to buying a house is lack of knowledge of existing programs. The committee and staff would work with REALTORS to promote the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority and U. S. Department Of Agriculture mortgage and down payment assistance programs. Homes bought with these programs count as state defined affordable housing. The general statutes municipal powers allow the creation of a housing trust fund. All towns in Connecticut are in a unique position they have found money in the form of COVID relief funds. And I recognize that most of the money is going towards building the new senior community center and I completely agree with this. It's recommended that a housing trust fund be established with an initial deposit from the COVID relief funds if there's any remaining and subsequent deposits could come from the annual budget if we chose to fund that in there or end of the year transfers of surplus funds.

We should be applying for small cities community development block grants, funding for money to fund the housing trust fund for housing rehabilitation and modification for low and moderate income owners and tenants. In considering Andover's age demographics, helping seniors comfortably age in place will be a huge issue to avoid social isolation. A safe and affordable home is critical, but also to assist seniors with aging in place it's critical that the town continues to provide support programs to maintain a good quality of life. These include the senior centers programming for all types of seniors, meals on wheels, dial a ride, visiting nurse program, and handyman services for small jobs within their homes. To help further affordable housing, we should consider tax abatement programs as allowed under the general Connecticut statutes. Next, we should be looking at modifying the existing housing stock. A recent AARP survey found eighty percent of seniors would like to remain in their homes and age in place. Consider direct grants from the housing trust fund and the small cities eligible grants to encourage low to moderate income qualified seniors to modify their homes to allow aging in place. This might be single floor living, bathroom modifications, ramps, and or to create affordable accessory units for extra income from a relative or a caregiver.

And the housing trust fund that could be paid back for many loans that we give out when the house is eventually sold by the people getting the loans. We could create a program which creates affordable accessory dwelling units by creating a direct grant housing trust fund in small cities, community development grant, block grant eligible or tax abatements.
